outputs.L1:
**Editor's note:** Carly Fiorina is chief executive of Carly Fiorina Enterprises and former chief executive of HP. She served as an adviser to Sen. John McCain's presidential campaign last year. In this commentary, Fiorina argues that public outrage over Wall Street pay is justified, but that salaries should not be set by government.

**(CNN)** -- Americans are outraged over excessive CEO pay and perks—and that outrage is entirely justified, particularly when American taxpayers are footing the bill. Our capitalist system functions best when transparency and accountability prevail, yet Wall Street has demonstrated far too little of either.

Inevitably, the president and Congress are now seeking to address taxpayer anger and, as President Obama recently declared, to restore some measure of "common sense" to CEO compensation. The proposed solution caps top executive pay at $500,000 for institutions that have received bailout funds.

Though this reaction is understandable, I do not believe it is the answer. For one, it is arbitrary: Why $500,000 rather than $400,000 or $600,000? For another, it is incomplete, applying only to institutions that will receive further government assistance going forward. Above all, our economy is not strengthened when the government determines the worth of each job. In America, we entrust that task to the markets.

So what is the answer?

To strengthen transparency, every aspect of CEO pay and perks should be fully disclosed on a regular basis. This should encompass airplanes, cars, golf-club memberships, bonuses, stock options, retirement plans, and salaries—in short, everything a reasonable person would consider part of a CEO's reward package.

To strengthen accountability, every aspect of CEO compensation should be subject to an annual shareholder vote. Ultimately, it is the owners of a company who must decide whether a CEO's rewards are justified by that CEO's performance. And because the American taxpayer is now a partial owner of many companies, the government may cast a vote as well—in some cases, a very sizable one.

In addition, "clawback provisions," which require a CEO to return compensation to shareholders when promised results are not delivered, should become standard practice.

Finally, when a company comes to Washington seeking American taxpayer money, it is an admission that mistakes have been made and major bets have failed. In such circumstances, these CEOs should be prepared to tender their resignations, along with those of their boards. To earn a bailout, a CEO and board must be held accountable.

We should not weaken our economy in the very act of trying to repair it. These are difficult times. President Obama has characterized our current situation as a "crisis" and an impending "catastrophe." In such times, action is required. The key is to take measures that provide short-term relief while remaining sensible for the medium and long term. Too often, our politicians respond to crisis and public anger by overreaching, thereby creating new and unforeseen problems that become apparent only with the passage of time.

In this country, the opportunity to be rewarded for taking prudent risk is fundamental to our economic vitality and strength. Let us not sacrifice that essential principle in our outrage over Wall Street greed and excess.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Carly Fiorina.*

**Editor's note:** Carly Fiorina serves as chief executive of Carly Fiorina Enterprises and previously led HP as its chief executive. During the past year, she advised Sen. John McCain's bid for the presidency. According to Fiorina, public anger over Wall Street compensation makes sense, though government should not be the entity determining pay levels.

**(CNN)** -- Across the country, people are furious about the lavish salaries and benefits handed to corporate CEOs. That anger is warranted, especially in cases where the tab is being picked up by American taxpayers. Our free-market economy functions most effectively when openness and responsibility are present—two qualities that have been in short supply on Wall Street.

Predictably, both the president and lawmakers are now trying to address taxpayer frustration and bring back a measure of "common sense," to borrow President Obama's recent phrase, to executive earnings. Their suggested fix would place a ceiling of $500,000 on the pay of senior executives at firms that have accepted rescue funds.

While I understand the impulse behind it, I don't believe this is the solution. The figure is random—why settle on $500,000 rather than $400,000 or $600,000? It's also partial, since it covers only firms that will seek additional federal help down the road. Moreover, our economy isn't served when the government dictates the value of each position. Here in America, we entrust that task to the marketplace.

So where does the answer lie? To boost openness, every element of a CEO's pay and perks ought to be laid out completely and routinely. That means aircraft, automobiles, golf-club dues, bonuses, stock options, pension arrangements, and base pay—essentially anything a reasonable observer would count as part of a CEO's total compensation.

To boost accountability, shareholders should get an annual vote on every component of a CEO's earnings. In the end, it falls to a company's owners to judge whether a chief executive's rewards match his or her results. And since American taxpayers now hold a partial stake in numerous firms, the government too can cast a vote—occasionally a very substantial one.

On top of that, "clawback provisions"—which obligate a CEO to hand back pay to shareholders when the promised outcomes fail to materialize—should become the norm.

Lastly, any company that approaches Washington seeking taxpayer dollars is effectively conceding that errors were committed and large gambles collapsed. In such circumstances, these executives should be ready to offer up their own resignations along with those of their boards. Receiving a bailout should carry a price: accountability from both the CEO and the board.

We must avoid damaging our economy in our efforts to repair it. These are trying times. President Obama has labeled our present predicament a "crisis" and a looming "catastrophe." Circumstances like these demand action. The challenge is to pursue steps that provide immediate relief while remaining wise for the medium and long haul. All too frequently, our elected officials respond to emergencies and public fury by going too far, generating fresh and unexpected troubles that surface only over time.

In this nation, the chance to be rewarded for taking sensible risks lies at the heart of our economic strength and dynamism. Let's not sacrifice that core principle amid our outrage over Wall Street's greed and excess.

The views expressed in this commentary belong exclusively to Carly Fiorina.

# On Executive Compensation and the Limits of Government Intervention

The public anger directed at excessive CEO compensation is entirely understandable, and in many cases fully justified. When corporations falter so badly that they require taxpayer-funded bailouts to survive, ordinary citizens have every right to question why the executives who steered these companies toward failure should continue to collect enormous paychecks. There is something deeply offensive about a system in which the people whose decisions necessitated a public rescue are rewarded with sums that most Americans could scarcely imagine earning in a lifetime. The outrage, in short, reflects a legitimate sense that something has gone wrong.

Yet acknowledging the validity of this frustration does not mean that every proposed remedy deserves our support. The government's plan to cap executive salaries at $500,000 is a case in point. However satisfying such a limit might feel in the moment, it suffers from serious flaws that make it a poor solution to a real problem.

## The Problems With a Salary Cap

First, the figure itself is arbitrary. Why $500,000 rather than $400,000 or $750,000? There is no principled basis for selecting this particular number, and any threshold chosen by political fiat will inevitably reflect momentary sentiment rather than sound economic reasoning.

Second, the cap is incomplete. Executive compensation is rarely composed of salary alone. It includes bonuses, stock options, deferred compensation, perquisites, and a host of other components. A rule that limits base salary while leaving these other channels untouched invites creative circumvention and addresses only a fraction of the total picture.

Third, and most fundamentally, a government-imposed cap places decisions that properly belong to the market in the hands of politicians and regulators. The appropriate level of compensation for any given executive depends on countless factors—the difficulty of the role, the talent available, the performance delivered—that are far better assessed by those with a direct stake in the enterprise than by lawmakers applying a one-size-fits-all rule.

## A Better Path Forward

Rather than dictating outcomes, the government should focus on improving the conditions under which compensation decisions are made. Two reforms stand out.

The first is transparency. Companies should be required to provide full disclosure of every component of executive compensation—salary, bonuses, stock awards, options, benefits, and any other form of reward. When the true scope of a compensation package is laid bare for all to see, the discipline of public scrutiny does much of the work that a blunt cap cannot.

The second is accountability. Shareholders should have the right to vote annually on executive compensation. And where taxpayers have injected public funds into a company, they too become partial owners and should be counted among those with a voice in these decisions. Such votes ensure that those who bear the consequences of a company's performance have a meaningful say in how its leaders are paid.

## Letting Owners Decide

The virtue of this approach is that it locates the decision where it belongs: with the owners of the enterprise rather than with the government. Owners are the ones best positioned to judge whether a chief executive's rewards genuinely match his or her performance. By strengthening transparency and enhancing accountability, we equip them to make that judgment wisely—and we address the legitimate grievance behind the public's outrage without resorting to the crude and counterproductive instrument of a government-mandated salary cap.

# Outrage Over CEO Pay Is Justified — But Government Salary Caps Are the Wrong Answer

*By Carly Fiorina*

Americans are angry about executive compensation, and they have every right to be. When a CEO walks away with tens of millions of dollars after running a company into the ground — while workers lose their jobs and shareholders lose their savings — something has gone deeply wrong. That anger is not envy. It is a demand for accountability, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

But taking public frustration seriously is not the same as endorsing every proposed solution. And the loudest proposal — having the government cap executive salaries — would do far more harm than good.

## The Problem Is Real

Let me be clear about where I stand. Having led a major corporation, I know firsthand that leadership carries enormous responsibility, and that compensation should reflect performance. What too often happens instead is that pay becomes disconnected from results. Boards approve lavish packages negotiated by compensation consultants who answer to the very executives they're evaluating. Golden parachutes reward failure. Bonuses get paid out even as a company sheds thousands of jobs.

This is a genuine failure of corporate governance. When executives are insulated from the consequences of poor decisions, the entire logic of a free market — that risk and reward go hand in hand — breaks down. The public sees this clearly, and their outrage is a healthy sign that Americans still believe rewards should be earned.

## Why Government Caps Fail

Here's the trouble: a government-imposed salary cap treats a symptom while ignoring the disease — and creates new problems in the process.

**First, caps don't work; they just move money around.** When Washington capped the deductibility of executive salaries above $1 million in the 1990s, companies simply shifted compensation into stock options and other vehicles. The result wasn't less pay — it was more complicated, less transparent pay, and arguably it encouraged the short-term stock manipulation that helped fuel later crises. Politicians declared victory; executives adapted overnight.

**Second, government has no business setting the price of talent.** The moment Washington decides what a CEO is worth, it claims the authority to decide what anyone is worth. Where does that logic stop? A one-size-fits-all cap can't distinguish between the executive who builds a company that employs thousands and the one who loots it. Bureaucrats in Washington are not equipped to make those judgments — and they shouldn't try.

**Third, caps drive talent and capital elsewhere.** We live in a global economy. Cap pay here, and the best leaders — and the companies they run — will find friendlier shores. We would be handicapping American competitiveness in the name of a political gesture.

## The Better Answer: Accountability, Not Control

The solution isn't more government control. It's more genuine accountability — the kind that markets are designed to deliver when they function properly.

That means empowering shareholders, the actual owners of these companies, with real "say on pay" votes that carry weight. It means demanding independent compensation committees that don't answer to the executives whose pay they set. It means full transparency, so that pay packages are disclosed in plain language and boards must defend them publicly. And it means ending the perverse incentives — the guaranteed bonuses and rewards for failure — that decouple pay from performance.

If a company wants to overpay its CEO, let it answer to its owners and the market, not to a federal formula. And when taxpayer money is involved — as it was in the bailouts — then yes, taxpayers are shareholders and have every right to demand restraint. That's not government overreach; that's ownership.

## Trusting Markets, Demanding Better

The genius of the American economy has never been that it prevents people from earning a lot of money. It's that it ties reward to results, and gives owners the power to hold leaders accountable. Where that link has broken, our job is to repair it — not to hand Washington a power it will inevitably abuse.

Public outrage is a powerful and legitimate force. Let's channel it toward reforms that strengthen accountability and restore the connection between performance and pay. Capping salaries would let politicians feel good while solving nothing. Americans deserve better than a symbolic gesture. They deserve a system that actually works.

*Carly Fiorina is the former CEO of Hewlett-Packard.*

# Real Accountability Means More Than Just Capping Pay

*A commentary from the perspective of a former Hewlett-Packard chief executive*

When President Obama announced this week that top executives at companies receiving taxpayer bailouts would face a $500,000 salary cap, the political appeal was obvious. Americans are angry—and rightfully so. They've watched their tax dollars flow to institutions whose leaders made catastrophic decisions, and many of those same leaders continued collecting extraordinary compensation. The public wants accountability. So do I.

But as someone who has sat in the chief executive's chair and wrestled with the real mechanics of running a large enterprise, I believe we should be honest about what this pay cap will and won't accomplish.

## The Problem With a Simple Cap

A $500,000 ceiling makes for a powerful headline, but it addresses symptoms rather than causes. The financial crisis wasn't fundamentally about executives being paid too much. It was about executives being paid the wrong way—rewarded for short-term gains while the long-term risks they created were invisible, ignored, or passed on to shareholders and, ultimately, taxpayers.

A rigid salary cap risks two unintended consequences. First, it may drive the most capable talent away from precisely the institutions that most need turnaround expertise. The banks and firms taking public money need to recover so taxpayers can be repaid. That requires strong leadership. Second, a cap on base salary invites creative workarounds—deferred compensation, restructured stock grants, and other mechanisms that obscure rather than clarify how much leaders actually earn.

If our goal is genuine accountability, we should focus less on the number and more on the structure and visibility of executive pay.

## Transparency as the First Principle

In my experience, sunlight is the most effective discipline in corporate governance. I would propose that any firm accepting taxpayer support be required to disclose executive compensation in plain, comprehensive terms—not buried in footnotes and proxy statements that require a specialist to decode.

Every American who helped fund these bailouts deserves to see, in a single clear document: what each senior executive earns, how that pay is structured, what performance targets trigger bonuses, and what happens to that compensation if the company fails to meet its obligations.

Transparency changes behavior. When leaders know their pay decisions will be examined openly by shareholders, employees, and the public, they make more defensible choices. A cap can be gamed. Genuine disclosure is much harder to escape.

## Tie Pay to the Taxpayer's Recovery

Here is a principle I believe should be non-negotiable: no executive at a bailed-out firm should realize significant personal gain until the taxpayer has been made whole.

Rather than capping salary, structure compensation so that meaningful rewards are deferred and contingent. Pay bonuses in restricted stock that cannot be sold until the government's investment has been repaid with a return. Institute genuine "clawback" provisions so that compensation tied to results can be recovered when those results prove illusory. Align the executive's financial future with the public's investment.

This approach does something a salary cap cannot: it keeps talented leaders motivated to succeed while ensuring they succeed *with* the taxpayer, not at the taxpayer's expense.

## Strengthen the Boards

Ultimately, executive compensation is the responsibility of a company's board of directors. Too often during this crisis, boards functioned as rubber stamps rather than genuine stewards of shareholder—and now public—interest.

Firms receiving federal assistance should be required to demonstrate that their compensation committees are truly independent and that they possess the expertise to evaluate risk, not just reward. Government need not run these companies. But it can reasonably insist that the people entrusted with oversight actually provide it.

## Accountability Runs Both Ways

Finally, a word of caution. Government now finds itself in the unusual position of both regulator and investor. That is a difficult balance. If Washington is going to demand accountability from the businesses it supports—as it should—it must also hold itself accountable for spending these funds wisely and providing a clear path for taxpayers to be repaid.

The American people understand fairness. They don't begrudge success honestly earned. What they cannot abide is a system where leaders prosper while the institutions they run collapse and ordinary citizens absorb the cost.

A $500,000 cap responds to that anger. But real reform requires more than a number. It requires transparency, structural alignment between pay and performance, empowered boards, and shared accountability. That is how we restore not just balance sheets, but public trust.

---

*The views expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.*

# The Market, Not Washington, Should Set Executive Pay

*Editor's Note: The following opinion piece was submitted by Margaret Ellsworth, a former corporate governance consultant and adjunct fellow at a market-oriented policy institute. The views expressed are her own and do not necessarily reflect those of this publication.*

---

Every few years, when a corporate scandal erupts or a CEO walks away with a golden parachute after steering a company into a ditch, the calls grow louder: Washington should cap executive compensation. It is an understandable impulse. Watching a chief executive collect tens of millions while workers are laid off offends our basic sense of fairness.

But the solution to bad pay practices is not to hand politicians a red pen and let them redesign the compensation of every public company in America. The solution is to make the market work better—through transparency, accountability, and the rightful authority of the people who actually own these companies: the shareholders.

## Why Salary Caps Fail

Government-imposed pay ceilings sound satisfying but deliver poorly. They assume that a legislator in Washington understands the labor market for a semiconductor executive or a pharmaceutical CEO better than the board that competes to hire one. Talent is global and mobile. Cap compensation at an American firm, and the best leaders may decamp to private equity, foreign competitors, or startups unconstrained by such rules.

Caps also invite creative evasion. Restrict cash salaries, and compensation migrates into perks, deferred arrangements, and offshore structures—often less transparent than what we have now. History shows that rigid rules rarely reduce total pay; they merely rearrange it into forms harder to scrutinize.

Most fundamentally, a cap severs the link between pay and performance. A one-size-fits-all ceiling rewards the mediocre executive who bumps against it and punishes the exceptional one who would have earned every dollar by creating billions in value. That is precisely backward.

## A Better Framework: Ownership, Accountability, Sunlight

Free-market principles do not mean "anything goes." They mean aligning incentives so that self-interest serves the common good. Three reforms do exactly that.

**First, empower shareholder votes.** The owners of a company should have a binding say on how their executives are paid. "Say on pay" votes exist, but too many are merely advisory. Strengthening them—giving shareholders real authority to reject excessive packages—puts the decision where it belongs: with the people whose capital is at stake. This is not regulation imposed from outside; it is the market's own governance mechanism functioning as it should.

**Second, mandate robust clawback provisions.** When compensation is awarded on the basis of results that later prove to be fraudulent, overstated, or achieved through reckless risk-taking, companies should be able—indeed, required—to recover that money. Clawbacks discipline behavior at the source. They tell executives that pay is contingent on genuine, durable performance, not on quarterly illusions that unravel later. This aligns the executive's downside with the shareholders' downside.

**Third, require full and clear disclosure.** Sunlight remains the best disinfectant. Compensation packages should be disclosed in plain language, with the ratio of executive to median worker pay, the performance metrics used, and the true value of every stock grant and perk laid bare. When pay is visible, embarrassing excess becomes its own corrective. Shareholders, employees, customers, and the press can all render judgment—and that judgment carries weight.

## The Conservative Case for Reform

Some defenders of business reflexively oppose any change to executive pay practices. That is a mistake. Crony arrangements—boards stacked with the CEO's friends, compensation consultants who tell clients what they want to hear, packages that reward failure—are not free-market capitalism. They are a corruption of it. Defending genuine markets requires rooting out the rot that gives capitalism a bad name and hands ammunition to those who would replace it with government control.

The choice, then, is not between unchecked excess and heavy-handed caps. It is between a market disciplined by its own owners and a market managed by bureaucrats. The former harnesses knowledge, competition, and accountability. The latter substitutes political guesswork for economic judgment.

We should trust the owners of American enterprise to govern their own companies—armed with the tools of voting power, clawbacks, and transparency—rather than outsource that duty to Washington. That is how a free society keeps both its capitalism and its conscience.

---

*Margaret Ellsworth writes on corporate governance and financial regulation. She can be reached through this publication's opinion desk.*

While ordinary workers watch their paychecks stretch thinner against rising costs, the average CEO of a major American company now earns roughly 300 times what their typical employee takes home. When a chief executive walks away with a golden parachute after running a company into the ground, the outrage isn't just understandable—it's justified.

But righteous anger makes for poor policy. The solution to excessive executive compensation isn't a new federal bureaucracy dictating salaries from Washington. It's a market that actually functions the way markets are supposed to: with accountability, transparency, and genuine consequences.

## Why Government Pay Caps Backfire

We've tried the heavy-handed approach before. When Congress capped the tax deductibility of executive salaries above $1 million in the 1990s, companies simply shifted compensation toward stock options and performance bonuses—arrangements that arguably fueled even more reckless short-term risk-taking. Price controls, whether on gasoline or executive pay, tend to produce workarounds, unintended consequences, and distortions that hurt the very people they aim to protect.

Government simply lacks the information to determine what any individual executive is worth. A talented turnaround specialist who saves thousands of jobs may genuinely be worth tens of millions. A mediocre caretaker collecting the same sum is being robbed—but that's a judgment the company's owners are far better positioned to make than a congressional committee.

## Give the Owners Real Power

Here's the uncomfortable truth: the real problem isn't that markets set CEO pay. It's that the market for executive compensation is broken. Corporate boards, often stocked with the CEO's allies and advised by consultants incentivized to justify ever-higher packages, approve compensation with too little accountability to the shareholders who actually own the company.

The fix is to strengthen ownership, not override it. Several concrete reforms would help:

**Mandatory annual "say-on-pay" votes.** Shareholders should vote every single year on executive compensation packages. While such votes currently exist in weakened, sometimes non-binding forms, they should be annual, clear, and consequential. When owners can regularly and visibly register disapproval, boards face real pressure to justify their decisions.

**Give binding force to shareholder rejection.** A "say-on-pay" vote that boards can ignore is theater. When a significant majority of shareholders rejects a pay package, boards should be required to revise it—putting genuine teeth into ownership rights.

**Require bailout CEOs to offer their resignations.** This is the clearest principle of all: if a company becomes so mismanaged that it requires taxpayer money to survive, its chief executive should be required to tender their resignation to the board. The board may choose to keep them if that leadership is genuinely essential to recovery—but the presumption should flip. You do not get to preside over failure, accept public rescue, and pocket a fortune as though nothing happened. Capitalism without the possibility of failure isn't capitalism; it's a rigged game.

**Claw back pay tied to phantom performance.** When compensation is awarded based on earnings that later prove fraudulent or are restated, that money should be recoverable. Executives should share in the downside, not just the upside.

**Radical transparency on pay ratios and structures.** Sunlight remains the best disinfectant. Requiring plain-language disclosure of how pay is structured, how it compares to the workforce, and what performance actually justifies it lets shareholders and the public make informed judgments.

## Accountability, Not Central Planning

Notice what these proposals have in common. None of them empower a government official to declare that a CEO earns too much. Instead, they empower the people who actually have a stake in the answer—the shareholders, including the millions of ordinary Americans whose pension funds and retirement accounts make them corporate owners whether they realize it or not.

This is the conservative case for reform that also happens to be the populist one. Real markets punish failure. Real markets demand that risk-takers face consequences. What we've had instead is a system that privatizes the gains and socializes the losses, where a well-connected executive class enjoys the rewards of success and the protections of a safety net when they fail.

The anger at excessive CEO pay is legitimate. But we should channel that anger toward restoring the discipline of the market, not replacing it with the discretion of politicians. Let the owners set the price. Just make sure they finally have the power to say no.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a political opinion article in the voice of a business executive and former McCain adviser critiquing Obama-era executive pay caps during the financial crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Perils of Government-Mandated Pay Caps

*By a business executive and former economic adviser to Senator John McCain*

When the Obama administration announced sweeping restrictions on executive compensation at firms receiving federal bailout funds, it was met with predictable applause. In the heat of the financial crisis, with public anger justifiably high, capping the pay of Wall Street executives seemed like an act of moral clarity. But governing by public sentiment, however satisfying in the moment, rarely produces sound policy. And these pay caps, I'm afraid, are a case study in good intentions producing counterproductive results.

## The Populist Temptation

Let me be clear: I share the frustration many Americans feel. When institutions that helped precipitate this crisis come to taxpayers with hat in hand, only to reward the very executives who steered them toward the rocks, something has gone deeply wrong. Accountability matters. I spent a campaign arguing that free markets carry responsibilities alongside their freedoms.

But there is a difference between demanding accountability and having Washington set salaries. The administration's compensation czar—a phrase that ought to give any conservative pause—now holds unprecedented power to determine what individuals may earn. This is a remarkable expansion of federal authority, and we should be wary of the precedent it sets.

## Talent Flees Restriction

Here is the practical problem the cheering crowds overlook. The firms receiving assistance need their most capable people now more than ever. Turning around a distressed institution, unwinding toxic assets, and restoring solvency requires exceptional talent. Yet by capping compensation, we are handing our healthiest competitors—and foreign banks unbound by these rules—a recruiting advantage.

The best performers will simply leave for firms without caps. What remains? Precisely the institutions taxpayers have the greatest stake in recovering will be hollowed out of the very people needed to repay us. We have created an incentive structure that undermines our own investment.

## The Better Path

Reform executive pay? Absolutely. But do it through the mechanisms markets and governance provide. Strengthen the hand of shareholders. Empower boards to tie compensation to genuine long-term performance rather than short-term risk-taking. Reform the perverse incentives that rewarded executives for gambling with other people's money. These are conservative solutions—market solutions—that address the actual disease rather than treating a symptom for political credit.

John McCain understood that leadership sometimes means telling people what they don't want to hear. The honest truth is this: government price controls on labor have failed everywhere they've been tried, whether on gasoline in the 1970s or wages in countless economies since. Human capital is no exception.

## A Warning Worth Heeding

We are in a moment when the temptation to expand government reach seems boundless, each intervention justified by the emergency of the day. But emergencies pass, and the powers we grant tend to remain. Today it is bailout recipients whose pay is capped. What is the principle that stops this authority from expanding to firms that never took a dime?

I do not doubt the administration's sincerity. I question its judgment. In our rush to punish, we should take care not to cripple the very recovery on which all of us—executives and autoworkers, shareholders and taxpayers—now depend.

---

*The author served as an economic policy adviser during the 2008 presidential campaign and has spent three decades in corporate leadership.*
